title: "Oscillations"

# Introduction to Oscillatory Motion
- Motion in a which a body displaces to and fro about a mean position, repeatedly.

## Important Terms
1. *Mean position*: The position of the body at the instant of time when the motion is at equilibrium.
2. *Amplitude (A)*: The largest displacement of the body from the mean position.
3. *Frequency ($\nu$)*: The number of oscillations per unit of time.
4. *Time Period (T)*: The time taken for one complete oscillation.
5. *Angular Frequency ($\omega$)*: The angular speed of the phasor representing the oscillation.

## Types
- Free Oscillations, Damped Oscillations, and Forced Oscillations.

# Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)

- Oscillatory motion in which the acceleration of the body ($a$) is proportional to the negative of its displacement ($x$) from its mean position.

$$
\text{i.e. } a \propto -x
$$

::: {.callout-note}

For angular SHM, the expression is instead written as:
$$
\alpha \propto -\theta
$$
Where $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration and $\theta$ is the angular displacement.

:::

The above equation can be rewritten as (by introducing a constant $\omega^2$):

$$
\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} \propto -x \implies \boxed{\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2x = 0}
$$ {#eq-shm-de}

The solution of this differential equation is given by a sinusoidal function of the form:

$$
\boxed{x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)}
$$
Where, $A$ is the amplitude, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and $\phi$ is the starting phase angle.

From the value of $\omega$, we can find the time period of the oscillations as $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$.

## Spring-Block System

![Spring Block System](images/spring-block.svg){width=8cm #fig-spring-block-system}

- This is an example of linear SHM.

- The force on the mass is proportional to the negative of the displacement from the equilibrium position, according to Hooke's Law.

$$ 
F \propto -x \implies \boxed{F = -kx}
$$ {#eq-spring-force}

- $k$ is known as the spring constant of the spring.

The above equation can be rewritten as:

$$
ma = kx \implies \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \frac{k}{m}x = 0
$$

Comparing this with @eq-shm-de, we get:

$$
\boxed{\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \text{ and } T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}}
$$

### Combination of Springs

#### Series Combination

![Series Combination](images/spring-series.svg){width=8cm #fig-spring-block-system}

The total extension of the springs is equal to the sum of the extensions of the individual springs. i.e., $x = x_1 + x_2 + \dots$

From @eq-spring-force, we get $x = \frac{-F}{k}$. Thus,

$$
\frac{-F}{k} = \frac{-F_1}{k_1} + \frac{-F_2}{k_2} + \dots
$$

Since the force is identical for all springs, we can divide the above equation by $-F \, (= -F_1 = -F_2 = \dots)$ to get:

$$\boxed{
\frac{1}{k_{\text{eff}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2} + \dots}
$$ {#eq-spring-series}

Where $k_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective spring constant.

#### Parallel Combination

![Parallel Combination](images/spring-parallel.svg){width=8cm #fig-spring-block-system}

The total restoring force is equal to the sum of the forces exerted by the individual springs. i.e., $F = F_1 + F_2 + \dots$

From @eq-spring-force, we get $F = k_1 x_1 + k_2 x_2 + \dots$. Thus,

$$
k x = k_1 x_1 + k_2 x_2 + \dots
$$

Since the extension of all springs is equal to the displacement of the mass, we can divide the above equation by $x \, (= x_1 = x_2 = \dots)$ to get:

$$\boxed{
k_{\text{eff}} = k_1 + k_2 + \dots}
$$ {#eq-spring-parallel}

Where $k_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective spring constant.  

Learn more at: [LibreTexts Physics: The motion of a spring-mass system](https://phys.libretexts.org/Courses/Berea_College/Introductory_Physics%3A_Berea_College/13%3A_Simple_Harmonic_Motion/13.01%3A_The_motion_of_a_spring-mass_system)

## Torsional Pendulum

- This is an example of angular SHM.

- The pendulum consists of a disc having some mass, suspended by a torsion wire (usually made of spring steel) from a rigid support.

- Here, the restoring force is caused by the torsional strain on the pendulum rod when the disc is rotated from its mean position.

$$ \tau \propto -\theta  \implies \tau = -k \theta $$

> The above equation is essentially a torsional equivalent to Hooke's law.

- $k$ is known as the torsional constant of the wire.
